analysis.one_liner: Adds a 5.4% surtax on income over $1 million and repeals tax breaks for oil and gas companies to cut the deficit.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in March 2011 and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, where it received no hearing, no vote, and no further action before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would raise revenue for deficit reduction by adding a 5.4% tax on each dollar of income above $1 million (the threshold is $2 million for couples filing jointly). It would also end three tax provisions that benefit oil, gas, and geothermal producers: the deduction for intangible drilling costs, the percentage depletion allowance for oil and gas wells, and the domestic production deduction for oil and gas output. Nothing in the record shows any action after it was referred to the Senate Finance Committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers benefit in two ways if the bill passes: the deficit is reduced without program cuts that would hit low- and middle-income households, and the burden falls entirely on households earning above $1 million and on oil and gas producers. The bill's findings frame the choice as raising this revenue versus cutting programs like Pell Grants, Head Start, community health centers, and the Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Imposes an additional 5.4% tax on modified adjusted gross income above $1 million ($2 million for joint returns), applying to tax years beginning after December 31, 2010.
Repeals expensing and 60-month amortization of intangible drilling costs for oil, gas, and geothermal wells.
Repeals the percentage depletion allowance for oil and gas properties.
Denies the domestic production deduction for income from the production, refining, processing, transportation, or distribution of oil and natural gas.

The bill's stated purpose is deficit reduction that does not cut programs used by working families; its findings contrast the tax breaks it would end with proposed cuts to Pell Grants, Head Start, community health centers, and LIHEAP.

analysis.who_pays: The direct costs fall on individuals with incomes above $1 million and on oil, gas, and geothermal producers, who would lose the drilling cost deduction, percentage depletion, and the domestic production deduction. To the extent higher costs on oil producers are passed to consumers, some of the burden could reach gasoline prices.
analysis.who_pays_short: Millionaires and oil and gas companies

drawbacks.text: A surtax applied on top of existing federal taxes, and the repeal of depletion and drilling deductions, could reduce investment in domestic oil and gas production; the bill makes no provision to soften the transition for producers or consumers.

Economists generally note that corporate tax preferences like percentage depletion are ultimately shared between producers, investors, and consumers, so some share of the oil-and-gas revenue could surface in energy prices rather than being borne entirely by shareholders.
The bill is one-sided deficit reduction: it raises revenue but authorizes no spending cuts or new programs, so its deficit effect depends entirely on the revenue raised.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill raises revenue exclusively from the highest earners and a highly profitable industry, which makes its distributional profile strongly favorable to working households, and the oil and gas provisions were versions of reforms that had circulated in both parties at various points. Its main weaknesses are that a 5.4% surtax on income over $1 million is a blunt instrument that some argue could discourage investment or entrepreneurship at the margin, and that some share of the oil and gas tax changes could reach consumers at the pump. The trade-off is real but modest relative to the size of the deficit the bill is meant to address.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never held a hearing, marked it up, or sent it to the floor; it died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced on March 10, 2011, by Senator Sanders together with Senator Mikulski, and read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance the same day.
The cosponsor list shows two Democratic senators.
No further action appears in the bill's action history after the referral to Finance, meaning no hearing, no markup, no floor vote in the 112th Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Households earning above $1 million and oil and gas companies kept the tax breaks the bill would have repealed, and the programs the bill's findings cite as the alternative to this revenue — Pell Grants, Head Start, LIHEAP, and community health centers — remained subject to the funding pressure the bill sought to relieve. No one who would have benefited from the bill's deficit-revenue approach gained from its failure.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Millionaires and oil and gas companies

for.name: Sen. Bernard Sanders
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and its stated findings on March 10, 2011.

for.name: Sen. Barbara Mikulski
for.role: U.S. Senator (D-MD), original cosponsor introduced with Sanders
for.what_they_did: Joined Sanders in introducing the bill on March 10, 2011.

sides.party_line_note: The record shows only three senators in support, all identified with the Democratic caucus or independent, and no recorded opposition votes; the bill simply received no committee action, so no party-line split was ever tested.

industries.note: The bill repeals three long-standing federal tax preferences for the industry: the intangible drilling cost deduction, percentage depletion for oil and gas wells, and the domestic production deduction. The industry would face higher effective taxes; to the extent costs pass through, consumers could see some of it at the pump.
The drilling cost repeal also covers intangible drilling and development costs for geothermal wells, a narrower effect than on oil and gas but a real increase in tax burden for the sector.
A new 5.4% surcharge applies to modified adjusted gross income above $1 million ($2 million joint), which lands on roughly the top fraction of one percent of filers.
